title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The new National Security Science & Technology Strategy names undersea, space, and AI/autonomous systems as its top three priorities. Read quickly, that looks like a flat list of
text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The new National Security Science & Technology Strategy names undersea, space, and AI/autonomous systems as its top three priorities. Read quickly, that looks like a flat list of three coequal domains. It isn't. Undersea and space are physical domains. AI and autonomous systems are a technology category. Pairing them isn't redundant; it's the strategy explicitly stating which capability dictates our ability to operate in those specific environments. Both domains share a critical constraint: you cannot assume a reliable link back to a human. A UUV can't surface for a GPS fix, or burst-transmit a position report, without giving away exactly where it is. A satellite, light-seconds from ground control, cannot wait for a human in the loop to execute a dynamic defensive maneuver. In both cases, AI isn't a third priority alongside them — it's the fundamental precondition for the other two working at all. This points to a concrete positioning strategy. If your technical bet is a decision architecture built to operate without a link home — how it resolves conflicting sensor input, operates under uncertainty, and decides when to hold versus act — that architecture doesn't care whether the external physics involve water pressure or orbital mechanics. It's the same class of problem wearing two different sets of physics. Building and selling that decision layer as portable, domain-agnostic IP is what allows a company to sell into both halves of this strategy's hardest domains, rather than getting boxed into a single platform. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope;
text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope; NN verification tools exist, but they scale poorly and only cover narrow, pre-specified properties over bounded inputs, not the real world your vehicle actually flies through. The pattern (often called Simplex, after Lui Sha's original work at Illinois) is simple to state and hard to build correctly: run your high-performance ML controller as the primary. Run a much simpler, formally verifiable baseline controller in parallel — one that can't do the mission well, but can be proven never to violate the safety envelope. A decision module — the actual hard engineering problem — watches system state and switches to the baseline before the envelope is breached, not after. Get the switching logic wrong and you get two failure modes, both bad: switch too conservatively and your ML controller never gets to do anything interesting; switch too late and the baseline can't recover in time. The switching threshold has to be derived from your vehicle's actual dynamics and worst-case latency, not picked as a round number. This is also why RTA architecture keeps showing up in DoW flight test programs pairing aggressive ML controllers with certified safety systems and automatic recovery — the government isn't asking "is your AI good," it's asking "what happens in the 0.1% case, and can you prove it." If your pitch deck shows an ML controller with no separately-verified safety layer next to it, that's the first thing a government test team asks about — long before they ask about your accuracy numbers. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

text: Организация Saildrone разместила контент: The Chukchi Sea is one of the most demanding maritime environments in the world: Freezing temperatures, rough seas, ice, and extreme remoteness make sustained operations difficult and expensive—particularly when crews and ships have to remain on station for extended periods. Saildrone is operating there now, extending observation into areas where persistent presence is otherwise difficult to maintain. And occasionally, the onboard cameras capture something unexpected. These walruses were filmed recently during operations offshore of Alaska—at a respectful distance, of course. A fun reminder of what persistent maritime awareness can reveal when you are watching places that are otherwise very difficult to reach..

Autonomous maritime systems like Saildrone provide the intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities necessary to stay ahead of an adversary at sea and ashore. To outlast the threat requires range, endurance, and persistence—Saildrone is proving it has all three, 24/7/365, operations around the world. Thank you to Vice Adm.
